class.title: Who Else Is Logged In? Find and Remove Unknown Sessions
class.objective: Find every device logged into your email and Instagram, remove any you don't recognize, and make sure your recovery email and phone number are yours.
class.northStar: Last week I checked who else was logged into my accounts, and it took 3 minutes. Let me show you where to look.

block.name: The Hook
block.text: TODO: real incident from your research (who, what happened, what it cost them, what would have stopped it). Add the source in the Learn More list.
block.question: If someone you used to trust were still logged into your email right now, what could they see?

block.name: The One Thing
block.text: Today you'll learn to check who is logged into your accounts and kick out anyone who shouldn't be there.
This matters because an ex, a roommate, or anyone who once used your phone or laptop can stay logged in for months without you knowing.

block.name: Core Concept: Passwords vs. Sessions
block.text: Your password is the key to the front door. A session is someone who is already inside.
When you log in, the app remembers that device so you don't have to type your password again. That memory is a session, and it keeps working even after you walk away.
Changing your password doesn't always end other sessions. You have to sign them out yourself.
block.question: Why might someone still have access to your account even after you changed your password?

block.name: Real Examples: Real Alert or Fake?
block.text: A real security alert tells you a new device signed in and points you to your account's own settings page.
A fake one asks you to click a link and "verify" your account by typing your password or a code.
block.question: You get an email saying "New sign-in on Windows. Click here to verify it was you." How do you check if it's real without clicking the link?

block.name: Hands-On: Check Your Own Accounts
block.step: Google: open your Google Account, go to Security, then "Your devices". Look at every device and location listed.
Instagram: go to Settings, Accounts Center, Password and security, then "Where you're logged in".
Sign out of any device you don't recognize.
In both accounts, check that the recovery email and phone number are yours.
Take a screenshot of your device list. That's your proof you checked.
block.question: Did you find any device you forgot about? What would you have done if you didn't recognize it?

close.oneAction: Do the same check on one more account in the next 24 hours, like your bank, Snapchat, or school email.

q.text: You changed your Instagram password, but your ex's phone still shows under "Where you're logged in." What's true?

option.feedback: Changing your password doesn't always end sessions that are already open.

q.option: They were logged out automatically

option.feedback: This list shows active sessions, not just old history.

q.option: It's just an old record, so you can ignore it
They may still have access until you remove that session

option.feedback: Deleting the app on your phone doesn't affect a session on their phone.

q.option: Deleting Instagram from your phone fixes it

q.text: What is a "session"?

option.feedback: Your password is what you type; a session is what the app remembers after you log in.

q.option: Your password
A device the app remembers as logged in, so it doesn't ask for your password again

option.feedback: A session isn't a time limit; it can last for months.

q.option: The time you spend in the app each day

option.feedback: Recovery info helps you get back in; it isn't a session.

q.option: Your recovery email address

q.text: You get an email: "New sign-in detected. Click here and enter your password to secure your account." What should you do?
q.option: Don't click it. Open the app or website yourself and check your devices there.

option.feedback: Real alerts don't need you to type your password into a link. This could be phishing.

q.option: Click the link and enter your password right away

option.feedback: Ignoring it skips the check. Someone might really be logged in.

q.option: Ignore it, since alerts are usually fake

option.feedback: Replying shares nothing useful and confirms your email is active to scammers.

q.option: Reply and ask if it's real

q.text: Why should your recovery email and phone number be checked, not just your devices?

option.feedback: Recovery info matters for more than just forgotten passwords.

q.option: They only matter if you forget your password

option.feedback: Alerts are a side effect. The real risk is that whoever controls your recovery info can reset your password.

q.option: They control which alerts you get

option.feedback: Recovery info doesn't affect how fast an app runs.

q.option: They make the app run faster
Whoever controls them can reset your password and get back in

q.text: True or false: once you change your password, everyone else is automatically logged out of every app.

option.feedback: Many apps keep existing sessions open unless you sign them out yourself.

q.option: True
False

q.text: Last year you logged into your Google account on your roommate's laptop and never logged out. She has since moved out. What should you do?

option.feedback: Hoping she won't look isn't a plan. The session stays open until you end it.

q.option: Nothing, she probably won't look

option.feedback: Asking is fine, but you can't confirm she did it. Checking yourself is the only sure way.

q.option: Ask her to log out for you
Check "Your devices" in your Google Account and sign out of any device you don't recognize

option.feedback: A new account doesn't remove access to your old one, which still holds your emails.

q.option: Make a brand new Google account

q.text: Where in Instagram can you see every device logged into your account?

option.feedback: Your profile shows posts, not logged-in devices.

q.option: Your profile page
Settings, then Accounts Center, then Password and security, then "Where you're logged in"

option.feedback: Notifications show activity on your posts, not devices.

q.option: The notifications tab

option.feedback: Your direct messages don't list devices.

q.option: Your direct messages

q.text: Your device list shows a sign-in from a city you have never been to. What's the best first step?
q.option: Sign out of that session, then change your password and turn on two-factor authentication

option.feedback: Locations can be off, but an unknown one is worth acting on. Doing nothing leaves the door open.

q.option: Ignore it, locations are always wrong

option.feedback: Posting about it doesn't remove the person and can tip them off.

q.option: Post about it on your story to warn them

option.feedback: Deleting your account loses your data. Signing them out fixes the problem without that.

q.option: Delete your whole account

q.text: Your ex knows your recovery phone number because it's an old shared family plan. Why is that a risk?

option.feedback: The issue isn't calls, it's account access.

q.option: They can call you

option.feedback: A recovery number doesn't show your location.

q.option: They can see your location

option.feedback: It isn't about texts on its own. The number controls password resets.

q.option: They can read all your texts
Codes to reset your password can go to that number, letting them get back into your account

q.text: True or false: if you don't recognize a device in your list, it's safe to leave it as long as you have a strong password.

option.feedback: A strong password doesn't kick out someone who is already logged in.

q.option: True
False

q.text: How often is it a good idea to check who is logged into your important accounts?

option.feedback: Waiting for a problem means someone could have access for months first.

q.option: Only after something bad happens

option.feedback: Once is a good start, but new sessions can appear any time.

q.option: Once, and never again
Every few months, and any time a relationship, roommate, or job situation changes

option.feedback: Every hour is unrealistic. A regular habit is what matters.

q.option: Every hour

q.text: You get a real Google alert: "New sign-in on iPhone." You don't own an iPhone. What do you do?
q.option: Open your Google Account yourself, review the device, and sign it out if you don't recognize it

option.feedback: Real alerts are worth acting on. Ignoring it leaves someone else in your account.

q.option: Ignore it, Google makes mistakes

option.feedback: Replying to an automated alert does nothing.

q.option: Reply to the email asking who it is

option.feedback: Waiting gives them more time in your account.

q.option: Wait to see if it happens again

q.text: Which of these would show up as a session in your device list?

option.feedback: A text message isn't a login.

q.option: A friend texting you

option.feedback: Following you doesn't log anyone into your account.

q.option: Someone following you on Instagram

option.feedback: Viewing your public profile isn't a login.

q.option: Someone viewing your public profile
An old phone you sold that is still signed in to your account

q.text: After you sign out unknown devices, what else should you do to keep them out?

option.feedback: Your profile picture has nothing to do with access.

q.option: Change your profile picture
Change your password and turn on two-factor authentication

option.feedback: Making your account public gives away more information.

q.option: Make your account public

option.feedback: Unfollowing people doesn't stop logins.

q.option: Unfollow everyone

q.text: A coworker says, "You can tell someone's in your account because your phone gets slower." Is that a good way to check?

option.feedback: Phones slow down for many reasons. It tells you nothing about who is logged in.

q.option: Yes, a slow phone means someone is logged in

option.feedback: Battery life has nothing to do with account sessions.

q.option: Yes, battery drain is the best sign
No, the only reliable way is to check the device list in your account settings

option.feedback: You don't need a technician. The device list is free and built into the app.

q.option: No, only a technician can tell

q.text: Pushback: "I have nothing to hide, so it doesn't matter who's logged in." What's the best response?

option.feedback: Agreeing skips the real risks, like someone reading your messages or resetting your password.

q.option: "You're right, it doesn't matter"
"It's not about hiding things. Someone logged in can read your messages, see where you are, and lock you out of your own account."

option.feedback: Fear doesn't convince people. A clear reason works better.

q.option: "You'll get hacked for sure if you don't check"

option.feedback: Dropping the topic leaves them at risk.

q.option: "Okay, never mind"

q.text: Pushback: "Checking devices takes too long." What's the best response?
q.option: "It takes about 3 minutes, and you only need to do it every few months."

option.feedback: Exaggerating hurts trust. The check is quick.

q.option: "It takes an hour, but it's worth it"

option.feedback: Saying it's not needed is wrong. It is the main way to find unknown sessions.

q.option: "You're right, you don't need to"

option.feedback: Paying someone isn't needed. It's free and built into the app.

q.option: "Pay someone to do it for you"

q.text: Pushback: "If my ex were logged in, I'd get an alert, so I don't need to check." What's the best response?

option.feedback: Agreeing is risky. Alerts don't catch every session.

q.option: "True, alerts catch everything"

option.feedback: Alerts are useful. The point is they aren't enough on their own.

q.option: "Alerts are always fake, so ignore them"
"Alerts usually only show new sign-ins. If they were already logged in before, you may never get one."

option.feedback: Changing apps doesn't solve it. The same check applies everywhere.

q.option: "Just switch to a different app"

q.text: Teaching: you have 10 minutes to teach a friend this topic. What should you do first?

option.feedback: Definitions first lose people. Start with something they can see.

q.option: Explain what a session is in technical terms

option.feedback: Scary stories alone don't show them what to do.

q.option: Tell them every hacking story you know

option.feedback: Sending a link skips the part where they actually do it.

q.option: Send them a link and leave
Have them open their own device list right away so they can see who is logged in

q.text: Teaching: your friend finds a device she doesn't recognize and panics. What do you tell her?

option.feedback: Panicking doesn't help. There are clear steps to fix it.

q.option: "That's really bad, there's nothing you can do"
"Sign that device out now, then change your password and turn on two-factor authentication. That locks them out."

option.feedback: Deleting the account loses everything and isn't necessary.

q.option: "Delete your account right away"

option.feedback: Waiting leaves the person in her account.

q.option: "Wait and see if it goes away"
